questions.question: A death benefit is specified by the deterministic rule $b(t)=100(1+t)$, where $t\ge0$ is years from issue to payment. What does deterministic mean for this benefit rule?
options: The amount is the same at every possible payment time.
The death time itself is fixed by the benefit rule.
The present value must be independent of death time.
The amount is fixed once the payment time is known.

questions.question: A whole life death benefit starts at 100 and has a 2% compound bonus vested each completed policy anniversary. The contract pays only at death. What does a vested anniversary bonus change?
options: It creates an immediate annual payment to the insured.
It increases the eventual death-benefit amount.
It replaces the death payment by survival payments.
It postpones death settlement to the next anniversary.

questions.question: A whole life benefit has base amount 1 and annual compound bonus rate $j>0$, vested only on completed anniversaries. Death occurs at time $T$ with $0<T<1$ years. Which nominal benefit has vested?
options: $(1+j)^T$, where $0<T<1$ is death time.

questions.question: Let $T$ be continuous remaining lifetime, $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$, and $v$ the annual discount factor. A non-negative benefit rule $b(t)$ assigns the amount payable at time $t$. For settlement at the end of the death year, which present value is correct?

A death benefit has a 2% bonus that vests annually under annual settlement. The insurer now proposes payment at death instead. What additional rule is needed to determine the benefit at a death between anniversaries?
options: Whether a vested bonus is discounted separately from the base benefit.
Whether death timing can be replaced by its mean when valuing the policy.
Whether any partial-year bonus accrues before death.
Whether annual discounting is removed because payment occurs at death.

questions.question: A whole life benefit starts at 100, with 2% compound bonus vested only on completed anniversaries. Death occurs at time 3.4 and settlement at time 4. The annual discount factor is $v=0.9$. What is the present value?
A benefit paid at death time $T$ follows $b(t)=100(1+t)$ for $t\ge0$. Death occurs at $T=2.4$ and the annual discount factor is $v=0.9$. What is the realised present value?

A varying death benefit settles annually, paying 100 at time 1 or 200 at time 2. Continuous death occurs in the first year with probability 0.4 and in the second with probability 0.6. With discount factor $v=0.9$, what is the APV?
A whole life death benefit follows a deterministic non-negative rule $b(t)$ and has finite APV 80 on a fixed mortality and interest basis. Every benefit amount is doubled. What is the new APV?
A death benefit starts at 100 and receives a 10% compound bonus on each completed anniversary. Two anniversaries have been completed before death. What nominal benefit is payable?

Two non-negative benefit rules $b_1(t)$ and $b_2(t)$ pay at the same continuous death time $T$ under fixed discount factor $v$. Both APVs are finite. What is the APV of the combined rule $b_1(t)+b_2(t)$?
options: The sum only when the two death times are independent.
The product of the two APVs because both benefits pay.
The larger APV because only one death occurs.
The sum of the two APVs, without an independence assumption.

questions.question: A base-1 whole life benefit has annual bonus rate $j\ge0$, completed-year count $K$ and annual-settlement value $Z=v^{K+1}(1+j)^K$. Let annual effective interest be $i>0$, with $v=(1+i)^{-1}$. What happens if $j=i$?
options: $Z=1$ for every $K$.
$Z=v$ for every $K$.
$Z=v^{K+1}$ for every $K$.
$Z=(1+i)^K$ for every $K$.

questions.question: For a base-1 annual-settlement benefit $Z=v^{K+1}(1+j)^K$, let $K$ be completed remaining years; keep mortality and $v>0$ fixed. The bonus rate rises from $j_1$ to $j_2>j_1\ge0$, and both APVs are finite. If $\mathbb{P}(K\ge1)>0$, how do the APVs compare?
options: The APVs are equal because payment remains certain eventually.
The APV at the higher bonus rate is strictly larger.
The higher bonus APV is smaller because payment is later.
The APVs differ only if mortality probabilities also change.

questions.question: Under constant mortality force 1 and interest force 1 per year, a whole life benefit pays $b(t)=1+t$ at death time $t\ge0$. What is its APV?

A base-1 whole life benefit settles annually with annual bonus rate $j=0.1$ on each completed anniversary. One-year survival is constantly $p=0.5$, and annual discount factor is $v=0.8$. What is its APV?

Let continuous death time $T$ be uniform on $(0,1)$ and $0<v<1$. Two benefit rules are $b_1(t)=1$ and $b_2(t)=1+t(1-t)$ on $[0,1]$. How do their unit-contract APVs compare under annual settlement at time 1 versus settlement at death?
options: Annual APV is larger for rule 2; at-death APVs are equal.
Both settlement conventions give equal APVs for the rules.
Rule 1 has the larger APV under both settlement conventions.
Annual APVs are equal; at-death APV is larger for rule 2.

questions.question: A death benefit is specified by $b(t)=t$ at payment time $t\ge0$. Death time $T$ is uniform on $(0,1)$ and discount factor is $v=0.9$. Compare payment at death with payment at time 1 using this same rule. Why can annual settlement have larger APV?
options: The later payment amount increases enough to outweigh discounting.
A positive interest rate makes every later payment more valuable.
Annual settlement changes the probability of eventual death.
The two contracts have the same nominal amount at every death.

questions.question: A continuous death time has constant mortality force $\lambda>0$. At interest force $\delta\ge0$, a benefit $b(t)=\mathrm{e}^{\gamma t}$ is paid at death, where $\gamma\ge0$ is its growth rate. Which condition characterises finite APV across all allowed rate combinations?
options: $\gamma<\delta$.
$\gamma\le\lambda+\delta$.
$\gamma<\lambda$.
$\gamma<\lambda+\delta$.

questions.question: Death time $T$ is uniform on $(0,2)$ and interest force is $\delta=\log2$. Rule A pays 1 for $T<1$ and 3 for $T\ge1$; rule B reverses those amounts. Both pay at death and have mean nominal benefit 2. Which APV comparison is correct?
options: $\operatorname{APV}(A)-\operatorname{APV}(B)=1/(4\log2)>0$.
$\operatorname{APV}(B)-\operatorname{APV}(A)=1/(4\log2)>0$.
$\operatorname{APV}(A)=\operatorname{APV}(B)=2\mathbb{E}[2^{-T}]$.
$\operatorname{APV}(B)-\operatorname{APV}(A)=1/(2\log2)>0$.

questions.question: A base-1 annual whole life benefit uses survival probability $p=1/2$ each year, bonus rate $j=1/2$ and discount factor $v=0.9$. Discounted benefit at settlement grows with completed years because $v(1+j)=1.35$. What is its APV?
options: Infinite, since the discounted benefit grows.
$9/10$, finite.
$18/13$, finite.
$9/2$, finite.
